title: Network Basics
summary: Names, addresses, localhost, URLs and ports: hostname, /etc/hosts, ping, curl.
intro:
Computers talk to each other over networks. The internet is just a giant network of networks!
In this lesson you will learn how computers find each other: names, addresses, URLs and ports.
Good news: everything here works offline. We only talk to your own computer.
outro: Now you know the basics of networks: names, IP addresses, localhost, URLs and ports. In the next lesson you will run your own web server!

setup.content:
# Terminal Academy: hide curl's progress bar (a normal terminal does not show it either), but still show errors.
silent
show-error

steps.instruction: Every computer has a name. Print the name of your computer.
hints: A 'host' is a computer on a network. The command is hostname.
steps.explain: Every computer on a network has a name and an address. The address is called an IP address, and it looks like 192.168.1.20.

steps.instruction: Show the file /etc/hosts. It is outside your sandbox, but reading it is fine (just don't change it).
hints: Use cat with the full path of the file.
steps.explain: This file is like a tiny phone book: it maps names to addresses. The line 127.0.0.1 localhost means: the name localhost is the address 127.0.0.1, and both mean 'this computer itself'.

steps.instruction: Is anybody home? Send 2 pings to 127.0.0.1 (that's you!).
hints: -c 2 means 'count 2', so ping stops by itself after 2 tries.
steps.explain: ping sends a tiny message and waits for the answer. The time (in ms) shows how fast the answer came back. Without -c, ping never stops; then press Ctrl+C.

steps.instruction: A URL is the address of something, like a web page. Use curl to read page.html with a file:// URL.
hints: A URL has a scheme (http, https, file), then ://, then the place. For file:// the place is the FULL path of the file, and $HOME is the full path of your sandbox.
steps.explain: curl gets whatever a URL points to and prints it. With internet, curl https://example.com would print the code of a real web page, the same code your browser gets.

steps.instruction: One computer can run many services. Each one waits behind its own port number. Find the ports of ssh, http and https in the file /etc/services. (If your computer has no such file, just type skip.)
hints: A port is like a door number on a computer. Search the file /etc/services with grep.
steps.explain: ssh uses port 22, http uses port 80 and https uses port 443. So https://example.com really means: computer example.com, door 443.
